newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Even apes and tigers need dentists.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Even apes and tigers need dentists.

text.p: Even the King of the Jungle needs a fluoride rinse now and then.
He might even get strawberry flavor, which is what gorillas like best, said Dr David Regine, who cares for the teeth of lions, tigers, elephants, apes and other animals as Pittsburgh's zoo.

"Animal teeth are like human ones. Same problems, same jaw structure, same tissues. They need care," he said. Examining a sleeping gorilla's pearly whites with a hand-held dental mirror, he remarked, "These are some of the best teeth I've seen."

"There isn't much written about animal dentistry so not many people know about it," Regine said. Most people do not think animals require root canals, fillings, caps or fluoride rinses. But they develop many of the same dental problems as humans and need the same treatments. One exception: animals do not need dental floss, he said. Animal teeth are too close together for dentists to be able to use it.
Regine said animals sometimes break their teeth from gnawing on bones and rocks or from fighting or rough play. They also develop cavities when well-meaning zoo visitors throw them sugary treats.
"People do things like throw fruit to the animals. People mean well but that sometimes can cause problems," he said.
EVEN TREATS BEAVERS' TEETH

Regine, who has been a dentist for 17 years, works on the zoo's largest and fiercest inhabitants -- elephants, lions, and polar bears -- as well as the smallest such as beavers and baby foxes. He also has a dental office for people in Bridgeville, Pennsylvania, near Pittsburgh.
His work at the zoo is volunteer and the hours he spends there vary depending on how many animals need care.

Obviously it would be difficult to get an animal to sit still for a dental exam so zoo animals are sedated. The amount of sedation they receive depends on their body weight. Fiercer animals such as tigers are sedated with a dart gun after they are coaxed into a special holding area and are carried to the zoo's hospital on a stretcher.

Smaller, mild-mannered animals can be brought to an examining room and need only a dose of gas to make them sleepy. The animals lie on an examining table while Regine performs dental work and veterinarians examine the rest of their bodies.
He treats animal teeth using the same nasty instruments that humans loathe -- the noisy drill, the messy water pik and the suction tube that produces a feeling of cotton mouth.
So who are better patients, animals or humans? "It varies," Regine said. "For the most part animals are the most cooperative because they're out of it."
ANIMALS MAKE GOOD PATIENTS
He said animals also make good patients because their teeth and gums heal faster than human ones. He said some species have five or six generations of teeth, versus two for people.
Christy Hostetler, zoo spokeswoman, said the Pittsburgh Zoo uses a total of four volunteer dentists. She said the practice of using volunteer dentists was fairly common among U.S. zoos.
"There are people who specialise in animal dentistry but we would have to pay them," she said. "So for a non-profit organisation you'll often find volunteer dentists."

Regine started doing dental work at the Pittsburgh Zoo three years ago. At that time he was a volunteer diver at the zoo, which uses volunteers to clean the inside of a huge tank that is home to several nurse sharks.

When zoo officials heard he was a dentist, he was asked to treat an elephant suffering from an infected tusk. The elephant had to be put under with anaesthesia with the help of several specialists -- an interesting task, Regine said. "You can imagine what it's like trying to put an elephant under anaesthesia."
He removed the elephant's tusk and has been caring for the zoo's animals since.
"I love animals and there's an attachment that comes with this work," he said. "Anything I can do to help animals, I'll do it."
